newsitem.title: GERMANY: Military to discuss Zaire aid in Germany on Friday.
newsitem.headline: Military to discuss Zaire aid in Germany on Friday.

text.p: Military leaders from nations expected to send troops on a relief mission to Rwanda and Zaire will meet on Friday in Germany, Canada's military said on Thursday.

The meeting, which has been delayed since Wednesday, is to be held at the U.S. European Command in Stuttgart, which is the headquarters for U.S. operations in Europe and most of the Middle East and Africa.
It will be chaired by Canada, which is coordinating efforts to establish the multinational force.
A Canadian forces spokesman in Stuttgart said the meeting would begin at 1000 GMT at Kelly Barracks and that a news conference was expected to be held after the meeting.
"In general terms, the meeting will be held to determine and decide on the general scope of the mission," Canadian Navy Reserve Lieutenant Charles Brown told Reuters.

Military leaders from several nations including the United States, France, Britain and Canada were expected to attend the meeting, which was called to review plans for the mission after hundreds of thousands of refugees began returning to Rwanda.
Since last Friday, Hutu refugees have begun streaming into Rwanda, causing some nations, especially the United States, to question the need to put ground troops in eastern Zaire.

Hundreds of thousands of Hutu refugees have fled back into Rwanda to escape fighting between Zairean Tutsi rebels, supported by Rwanda, and soldiers from Rwanda's Hutu-dominated ex-army and militias, who organised the 1994 Rwandan genocide of minority Tutsis.
Canada on Wednesday said at the United Nations that most nations involved in the humanitarian crisis in Africa believed a military force was still needed to deliver aid.

Britain, France and Spain have all said the force is still required but Washington has cancelled plans to send combat troops to Zaire and instead begun preparing for an airlift in which the military will provide the logistics.
However, Canada's Deputy Foreign Minister Gordon Smith said on Wednesday that military planners needed to develop a range of options -- including not sending ground troops at all.
Smith made the comment after a series of meetings at the United Nations, one of which involved representatives from 60 countries, including nations who have volunteered troops.

The options, he said, ranged from convoys and air support that might not require ground troops to a scaled-down version of the original intervention plan that a week ago envisaged at least 10,000 soldiers in the region.
